steps.label: Conclusion (therefore)
steps.body: It is likely that this ancient society was still a hunter-gatherer society.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Even though there's evidence that they burned large areas of land, there is little evidence of (agricultural) cultivation after the fires.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This is a curious fact with two competing stories. The fact: this society burned large areas of land. The rival story: the burning cleared ground for planting, so the society was turning to large-scale agriculture. The author's story: the society was still hunting and gathering.

The author's only support is an absence: little evidence of cultivation after the fires. That is a fair point against the farming story, but it leaves a hole. If these people were hunter-gatherers, why were they burning large areas of land at all? Right now the burning has an explanation under the farming story and none under the author's.

Given that the society burned large areas of land, how could we still argue that it was farming? We could say crops were planted but left little trace, or that the land was burned for some other farming purpose. Nothing in the argument answers the basic question: what would hunter-gatherers want with a big fire?

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that gives hunter-gatherers a reason to burn large areas of land. That turns the burning from evidence for farming into something the author's story expects. A second acceptable shape: more evidence that the burning was not done to clear ground for planting. Answers about small fires, or about farming in other societies, will not do this work.

notes.body: A says that in many ancient cultures, agriculture came first and fire-clearing came later. That says nothing about why this society burned its land. If anything, it hints that a society clearing land with fire already farmed, which leans the wrong way. It gives no hunter-gatherer reason for the fires.

Cooking and heat explain campfires, not the burning of "large areas of land." Farmers cook and keep warm too, so this use of fire fits both stories equally. A strengthener has to explain the large-scale burning in a way the hunter-gatherer story predicts and the farming story does not.

C says fire releases the seeds of certain plants. That is a fact about plants, not about why this society burned land. The seeds are "inedible," so it does not give foragers a food reason to burn. And if fire helps plants spread, it might even suggest a planting motive. No link to hunter-gatherers, so no strengthening.

D supplies the missing reason. Hunter-gatherers are known to burn land to move animal populations from one area to another. Now the fires have an explanation that fits the author's story, and the lack of cultivation afterward is exactly what we would expect: the fires were for hunting, not planting. The burning stops counting as evidence for farming.

The move to repeat: when an argument picks one explanation for a fact over a rival, look for an answer that explains the fact under the author's story. A fact only the rival story can explain is a liability until an answer like D removes it.

E undercuts one possible farming motive: burning to enrich the soil. But the farming story in the stimulus is about clearing ground for planting, not adding nutrients, so E leaves it standing. And weakening a farming motive still gives hunter-gatherers no reason to burn large areas, which is what the argument needs.

why: PT157/158 register: em dashes, notes over 100 words that repeat themselves, and an Evaluate built on outside history instead of the gap (why hunter-gatherers would burn land).

steps.label: Conclusion (Thus)
steps.body: Schools should not require students to take courses in individual academic disciplines but should instead require them to take interdisciplinary courses.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Most problems in daily life can't be solved most effectively, if at all, by applying knowledge from any single academic discipline in isolation.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The premise is about problems: most daily-life problems need knowledge from more than one discipline. The conclusion is about courses: schools should require interdisciplinary courses instead of single-discipline ones. The gap is the jump from what problems need to how courses must be built.

Given that most daily-life problems need more than one discipline, how could we still argue that schools should keep single-discipline courses? Easy. Students could take several single-discipline courses and then combine what they learned when a real problem shows up. If students can do that combining on their own, interdisciplinary courses are not needed.

So the educator is assuming that students in single-discipline courses will not put their knowledge together on their own.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that shuts down that objection: students who take only single-discipline courses do not, or cannot, combine what they learned. A second acceptable shape links premise to conclusion directly: if daily-life problems need several disciplines, schools should teach across disciplines. A strengthener does not have to prove the conclusion. It only has to make it more likely.

notes.body: A says common sense usually solves daily-life problems. That does not tell us which kind of course better prepares students, so it cuts the same way against both. If anything, it makes all coursework matter less for daily life, which gives the educator's recommendation no help.

B gives a reason to keep the current system: most teachers do a better job with single-discipline courses. If teaching quality drops when schools switch, students might learn less under the educator's plan. That pushes against the conclusion, so it cannot strengthen it.

C answers the objection we built. Students who take only single-discipline courses "are rarely able to combine knowledge from those disciplines." Put that next to the premise: daily-life problems need knowledge from more than one discipline, and these students rarely put disciplines together. So single-discipline courses leave students short, and courses that combine the disciplines for them make sense.

The move: when a recommendation is built on a need, ask how the current approach might already meet that need. The answer that says it does not is the strengthener.

D says most students in single-discipline courses "can effectively solve many problems faced in daily life." If they already handle those problems, the case for switching gets weaker. D is the objection from the Evaluate step stated as fact, so it weakens.

E says most interdisciplinary courses are not designed to teach daily-life problem solving. If the courses the educator wants do not aim at that goal, switching to them looks less useful. That is a reason to doubt the plan, not to support it.

why: Goal used the Necessary Assumption negation test on a Strengthen question, Evaluate had a typo, and the C note carried em dashes and padding; the earlier D misquote is already fixed.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The psychological stress, not the physiological exertion, involved in talking causes one's blood pressure to rise.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Most people's blood pressure rises somewhat when they talk, but introverted people's BP rises even more than extroverted people's, and introverted people are more psychologically stressed when they're talking.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The psychologist presents a correlation:
```
more stressed by speaking (introverts)  ||  bigger blood pressure rise
```
Then the psychologist concludes that one causes the other: the stress of communicating drives the rise, not the physical work of producing speech.

That is a Curious Fact → Causal Explanation argument, so we check two things:
1. Is there an alternate explanation for why introverts' surges are bigger?
2. How plausible is the author's explanation?

Given the correlation, how could we still argue that physical exertion causes the rise? Maybe introverts and extroverts differ in some physical way when they talk, or in some health factor that changes how much their pressure moves. The bigger problem: whenever someone speaks, communicating and the physical act of speaking happen together. The argument never pulls them apart.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that separates communication from the physical work of speaking and shows blood pressure following communication. The ideal case: communication without vocal speech, or similar physical effort without communication. A second acceptable shape rules out an alternate explanation for why extroverts' surges are milder.

notes.body: A says blood pressure medication does not stop the rises during speech. That tells us the rise is hard to block, not what causes it. A rise driven by stress and a rise driven by physical exertion could both get past medication, so A favors neither cause.

B links a person's typical blood pressure to how much it rises under stress. It never separates stress from physical exertion. If anything, it opens an alternate explanation: if introverts had lower typical pressure, their surges could be bigger without speaking being any more stressful for them.

C says introverts often sense the rises when they talk. Noticing a change says nothing about what caused it. An introvert could feel the rise whether it came from stress or from the physical work of speaking, so C does not help the psychologist.

D builds the test we wanted. Signing is communication with no vocal speech production. Moving the hands for other reasons takes similar physical effort with no communication. Blood pressure rises for signing and shows "no change" for the other hand movements. With the physical effort held roughly constant, only communication changes, and blood pressure follows communication. That cuts down the physical-exertion explanation and supports the stress of communicating.

The move: when an argument picks between two causes that always show up together, the strongest support finds a case where they come apart and shows the effect tracking the author's cause.

E looks relevant because it is about extroverts and blood pressure, but it weakens. If extroverts are more likely to take blood pressure medication, the medication could be what keeps their surges mild. That is an alternate explanation for the very difference the psychologist credits to stress.

why: Evaluate used gendered pronouns for the psychologist, the Goal's example reversed the groups, and the notes ran long with em dashes; E's weakening route (medication) was never named.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Even if you have to pay more and even if you would never follow through on making a warranty claim if your pan broke, you should only buy a pan that has a warranty.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: If offering a warranty meant that a company would need to reimburse a bunch of customers when the product broke, then manufacturers wouldn't offer a warranty.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This premise is conditional. By contrapositive, it tells us something we know about every frying pan that offers a warranty.
```
if manufacturers  →  company doesn't think they
offer warranty       will have to reimburse many
```
So our author is saying that we should only buy pans that offer a warranty, because that means the manufacturer isn't worried about having to pay out a bunch of warranty claims.
Our author is assuming that "if they aren't worried about paying out claims, it's because the frying pan is high quality and they don't expect it to break down for a lot of people".
But maybe they're not worried because even though they anticipate many of them breaking, they don't think many customers will have the follow-through to claim the warranty.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for an answer that closes that gap: a pan that does not work well or last long really would cost its manufacturer, because many buyers would seek reimbursement. Then a warranty can only sit on a pan the manufacturer expects to hold up.

Notice who the conclusion is talking to: a buyer who would never bother to claim. So the answer has to be about other buyers. Their claims are what make the warranty mean something.

notes.body:
A says most people who buy a pan with a warranty "would seek reimbursement" if it failed. Now follow the chain. If the pan were bad, many buyers would claim, the manufacturer would have to reimburse many customers, and by the premise it would not offer the warranty. So a pan with a warranty is one the manufacturer expects to work well and last. That is why even a buyer who would never claim should buy it.

The move: when a premise says a party avoids a cost, check what makes the cost real. Here the cost depends on buyers actually claiming, and A supplies that.

B compares pans only "at the time of purchase." The argument cares whether a pan will keep working and last long, which is what a warranty is supposed to signal. A pan can match the others on day one and still fail in a year. B also says nothing about why manufacturers offer warranties, so it does not connect the premise to the conclusion.

C ties price to warranties. It does not show that a warranty means a good pan. The conclusion already accepts paying more, so learning that pans with warranties tend to cost more adds no reason to buy them.

D ties price to quality. The conclusion says to buy pans with a warranty, not expensive pans. Even if the priciest pans last longest, that gives no reason to prefer a pan with a warranty over one without at the same price.

E says most warranties "provide for full customer satisfaction." That describes what a claim gets you. But the buyer in the conclusion would never make a claim, so the warranty's terms do not matter to them. E also does not explain why a manufacturer would avoid putting a warranty on a bad pan.

why: Notes were padded with em dashes and capitals, the B note misread B (which says pans with warranties are at least as good, not equal) and called it a weakener, and the Goal did not name the answer.

steps.label: Claim
steps.body: Increasing the prison term for robbery won’t discourage people from committing robbery.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
There is no evidence here, just one claim. So our job is to find reasons to believe it.

Think about how a longer prison term is supposed to work. It deters only if a would-be robber knows the penalty, expects it to apply, and weighs it before acting. So the claim gets support from anything that breaks that chain: robbers who do not know the sentence, robbers who do not expect to be caught, robbers who are not weighing costs at all. It also gets support from a similar case where a longer term made no difference.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Four answers will give one of those reasons to believe a longer term would not discourage robbery. The answer we want gives none. Expect it to have no clear impact on what a longer term would do, or to cut against the claim.

notes.body: If many robbers are driven by "thrill-seeking and risk-taking," they are not carefully weighing costs, and a longer sentence may even add to the risk they enjoy. Either way, a bigger penalty is unlikely to stop them. That supports the claim.

B is an analogy. A longer prison term for embezzlement did not change how often that crime was committed. If longer terms failed to deter a similar crime, that is some reason to expect the same for robbery. It supports the claim, as far as the two crimes are alike.

C is about the past: robbery terms "have generally decreased in length recently." The claim is about what would happen if terms went up. Knowing that terms went down tells us nothing about whether raising them would deter anyone. C gives no reason to believe the claim, so it is the exception.

The move on Strengthen EXCEPT: list the kinds of support before reading the choices. Here that list was robbers who do not know the sentence, do not expect to be caught, or do not weigh costs, plus a similar case. The answer that fits none of them is the one to pick.

If most robbers believe "they will not get caught," they do not expect any sentence to apply to them. The length of a term they never expect to serve cannot weigh much in their decision. That supports the claim.
If most robbers "have no idea what the average sentence for robbery is," they would not notice a longer one. A penalty you do not know about cannot deter you. That supports the claim.

why: Evaluate said only that there was no argument, the Goal gave no shape for the four supporters, and the C note hedged and then overclaimed that C weakens.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: A recent study found that in each of the last ten years, the number of traffic accidents that resulted in death was greater during the day than during the night.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: It is more dangerous for an individual to drive during the day than during the night.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence counts fatal accidents: in each of the last ten years, more happened during the day than during the night. The conclusion is about risk to "an individual": driving by day is more dangerous for each driver.

Given that more fatal accidents happen by day, how could we still argue that night driving is just as dangerous? Count the drivers. If far more people drive during the day, the day could have more fatal accidents and still be safer per driver. A bigger total is not a bigger rate.

So the argument needs a reason the danger itself is higher during the day: something about daytime driving that raises the risk for each driver.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Four answers will strengthen by giving a day-specific risk: something that makes each daytime trip more dangerous, or each nighttime trip safer. The correct answer will not. Expect it to show no day-versus-night difference at all, so it cannot explain why the day is more dangerous.

notes.body: A gives a daytime-only hazard: only during the day do unsafe vehicles outnumber safe ones. Every daytime driver shares the road with more unsafe vehicles, so the higher daytime death count reflects real risk, not just more traffic. That strengthens.

B says there is less law enforcement during the day. Less enforcement plausibly means more reckless driving goes unchecked, which raises the risk for each daytime driver. That is a day-specific reason for the extra fatal accidents, so it strengthens.

C says people drive more cautiously at night. That makes each night trip safer than a day trip, which explains the extra daytime fatal accidents with something other than traffic volume. It strengthens.

D is the exception. More travelers per vehicle over the past ten years is a trend across day and night alike. It might raise deaths per accident, but nothing in D says the change hits daytime harder. Without a day-versus-night difference, it does nothing to show the day is more dangerous for an individual.

The move on a Strengthen EXCEPT built on a comparison: each strengthener has to favor one side of the comparison. An answer that applies equally to both sides cannot help.
E says people drive faster during the day. Higher speeds make crashes more likely and more deadly, and this applies only to daytime driving. That is another day-specific risk, so it strengthens.

why: Evaluate missed the count-versus-rate gap and called the conclusion evidence, the Goal and Evaluate used em dashes, and the four strengthener notes were bare tags.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Those persons who are perceived as forming opinions of others only after cautiously gathering and weighing the evidence are generally resented.

In short: appearing prudent gets you resented.
AP → R

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body:
It is imprudent to appear prudent.
AP → ~P

Here ~P means not prudent.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Line the two up. The premise starts at appearing prudent and ends at being resented. The conclusion starts at appearing prudent and ends at imprudent. Same start, different finish. Being resented shows up only in the premise, and imprudent shows up only in the conclusion, so the missing piece has to connect them:
R → ~P
In words: causing people to resent you is imprudent. Add that and the chain runs
AP → R → ~P
which is the conclusion.

The first sentence, that people want to be instantly and intuitively liked, explains why cautious people are resented. It is background. It never reaches the conclusion's new idea.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that says being resented, or causing resentment, is imprudent. The contrapositive would work too: anything prudent does not cause resentment. Reject answers that start from imprudent (a reversal), or that talk about acting instead of appearing, or being liked instead of being resented.

notes.body: A says people who act spontaneously are well liked. That is about acting spontaneously and being liked, not about appearing cautious and being resented, and it never mentions prudence. The gap is between resentment and imprudence, and A touches neither side of it.

B starts from imprudent people:
~P → acts instantly and intuitively
That puts imprudent on the trigger side, but we need to prove imprudent, so it has to be on the outcome side. B also talks about how people act, while the argument is about how they appear. It cannot finish the chain.

C says people resent those less prudent than themselves. That is about who gets resented, and it points at the less prudent, not the cautious people in the premise. It never says that being resented is imprudent, so the conclusion still does not follow.

D is about whether intuitive people know instantly when they like someone. The argument needs a link from being resented to being imprudent. D mentions neither resentment nor prudence, so adding it leaves the gap where it was.

E says it is imprudent to cause people to resent you:
R → ~P
Chain it to the premise: appearing prudent gets you resented, and causing resentment is imprudent, so appearing prudent is imprudent.

The move on Sufficient Assumption: find the idea in the conclusion that no premise mentions (imprudent), find the premise idea that never reaches the conclusion (resented), and pick the answer that joins them in the right direction.

why: A difficulty-4 Sufficient Assumption explained by margin diagrams: no Goal, verdict-only B and D notes, a one-line correct note, and an A note that misdescribed the choice.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Both premises use without. A sentence of the form no X without Y means X needs Y: X → Y.
```
IF → SI
GL → SI
```
Individual freedom requires social integrity. Pursuing the good life requires social integrity.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body:
```
IF → RL
```
Individual freedom requires the rule of law. The rule of law appears only here. No premise mentions it.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start from the conclusion's trigger, IF. The first premise takes us from IF to SI. Then we are stuck: nothing takes us from SI to RL. Supply that link and the chain runs
```
IF → SI → RL
```
which gives IF → RL.

The second premise, about the good life, is a distraction. GL also points to SI, so two arrows lead into SI and none lead out. The good life never connects to individual freedom, so it cannot help.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for SI → RL: there is no social integrity without the rule of law. Expect traps that use the right terms with an arrow pointing the wrong way: the link reversed (RL → SI), a premise reversed, or the conclusion reversed. Check the direction of every arrow.

notes.body:
A says there can be no rule of law without social integrity:
```
RL → SI
```
That is the link we need, backwards. With IF → SI and RL → SI, both arrows end at SI, so nothing carries us from IF to RL. Watch for this reversal on any chain question.

B says there can be no social integrity without the rule of law:
```
SI → RL
```
Hook it onto the first premise: IF → SI → RL, so IF → RL. That is the conclusion.

The move: when the conclusion has a term no premise mentions (the rule of law), the assumption must run from the end of the premise chain to that new term.

C says one cannot pursue the good life without the rule of law:
```
GL → RL
```
That helps only if we can get from IF to GL, and we cannot. The premise gives GL → SI, and nothing leads into GL. C would work only if the good-life premise were reversed (SI → GL).

D says social integrity is possible only if individual freedom prevails:
```
SI → IF
```
That reverses the first premise. It points back toward IF, and RL never appears, so the conclusion's new term is still out of reach.

E says there can be no rule of law without individual freedom:
```
RL → IF
```
That is the conclusion reversed. Assuming the reverse of what we want to prove does not establish it.

why: A difficulty-5 Sufficient Assumption explained only by arrow diagrams: no Goal, no prose on how B completes the chain, and no reason why the good-life premise and the reversal traps fail.
